html:
The Gregorian calendar is the reform of the old Roman Julian calendar ordered by Pope Gregory XIII in 1582. It is now the civil calendar of most of the world.

The Julian calendar, set up by Julius Caesar in 45 BCE, added a leap day every fourth year, giving an average year of 365.25 days. The true solar year is about eleven minutes shorter. Over the centuries the error added up to some ten days, so the spring equinox, and with it the date of Easter, drifted away from where the Church had fixed it in the 300s.

The fix, worked out by the astronomer Aloysius Lilius and the Jesuit mathematician Christopher Clavius, had two parts:

  • Drop ten days once: Thursday 4 October 1582 was followed by Friday 15 October.
  • Change the leap year rule: century years are leap years only if divisible by 400. So 1600 and 2000 were leap years; 1700, 1800 and 1900 were not.

The average year becomes 365.2425 days, close enough to be off by only a day in about 3,000 years.

Catholic states such as Spain, Portugal and the Italian states switched at once, as the Council of Trent had asked for the reform. Protestant and Orthodox countries were suspicious of a papal decree. Britain and its colonies changed only in 1752, dropping eleven days; Russia changed after the 1917 revolution, which is why the October Revolution is remembered in November. Many Orthodox churches still use the Julian calendar to date Easter.
sum: The Gregorian calendar is the reform of the old Roman Julian calendar ordered by Pope Gregory XIII in 1582. It is now the civil calendar of most of the world.
